s0101.literal: He then told the envoy: "The brothers of Gaozhou have risen high—all is the state's grace; now one should hurry to aid the capital in its peril—how can one play the bully on one's own?"
s0101.idiomatic: He told the envoy: "Gaozhou's brothers owe their rank to the throne. They should march to save the capital—not play petty kings."

s0102.literal: When the Founder came to relieve the capital and was about to reach Shixing, Wei then bound himself to him deeply.
s0102.idiomatic: When the Founder marched to relieve the capital and neared Shixing, Wei threw in with him wholeheartedly.

s0103.literal: Yu sent troops to attack Wei; the Founder aided him; Yu was defeated; the Founder made Wang Huaiming Inspector of Hengzhou and moved Wei to Interior Minister of Shixing.
s0103.idiomatic: Yu attacked; the Founder helped Wei and broke Yu. Wang Huaiming took Hengzhou; Wei was moved to interior minister of Shixing.

s0104.literal: When the Founder campaigned against Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi, Wei led troops across the mountains to aid the Founder.
s0104.idiomatic: On the Founder's campaigns against Cai Luyang and Li Qianshi, Wei crossed the ridge with troops to help.

s0105.literal: When Luyang and the others were pacified, Wei had merit; Emperor Yuan of Liang by regency commission made Shixing commandery into East Hengzhou and made Wei Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant for Direct Communication, Commander-in-Chief of East Hengzhou, Cloud-Banner General, Inspector of East Hengzhou, Baron of Xinfeng county, fief four hundred households.
s0105.idiomatic: When they were pacified he won merit. Emperor Yuan made Shixing into East Hengzhou and gave Wei the staff, direct-communication attendant, command of East Hengzhou, cloud-banner general, inspectorship, barony of Xinfeng, fief four hundred households.

s0106.literal: When Hou Jing was pacified, Emperor Yuan asked all the court ministers everywhere: "Now the realm is newly settled; we urgently need good men—each of you recommend whom you know."
s0106.idiomatic: When Hou Jing fell, Emperor Yuan asked the court: "The realm is new-settled. Name the men you trust."

s0107.literal: The ministers had none who answered.

s0108.literal: The emperor said: "I have already got one man."
s0108.idiomatic: The emperor said: "I already have one man."

s0109.literal: Attendant-in-Ordinary Wang Chan advanced and said: "I do not yet know who it is?"
s0109.idiomatic: Wang Chan stepped forward: "Who is it?"

s0110.literal: The emperor said: "Ouyang Wei is upright and has talent to steady the age; I fear the Inspector of Guangzhou Xiao will not be willing to send him."
s0110.idiomatic: The emperor said: "Ouyang Wei is upright and can steady the age—but Guangzhou's Xiao may not let him go."

s0111.literal: Editorial footnote marker 8. He then appointed Inspector of Wuzhou; soon he appointed Inspector of Yingzhou, wishing to have him leave the mountains; Xiao Bo detained him and he could not take up the commission.
s0111.idiomatic: [8] He was made inspector of Wuzhou, then of Yingzhou, to draw him out of the hills. Xiao Bo held him and he never took up the seal.

s0112.literal: Soon he was made Bearer of the Staff, Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of Hengzhou, Loyal Martial General, Inspector of Hengzhou, advanced to Marquis of Shixing county.
s0112.idiomatic: Soon he had the staff, scattered-cavalry attendant, command of Hengzhou, loyal-martial general, inspectorship, and was advanced to Marquis of Shixing.

s0113.literal: At that time Xiao Bo was at Guangzhou, troops strong and position weighty; Emperor Yuan deeply feared him and sent Wang Lin to replace him as inspector.
s0113.idiomatic: Xiao Bo at Guangzhou was strong and heavy. Emperor Yuan feared him and sent Wang Lin to replace him.

s0114.literal: Lin had already reached Little Gui Ridge; Bo sent his general Sun Yang to oversee the province, led all his subordinates to Shixing, and avoided Lin's edge.
s0114.idiomatic: Lin reached Little Gui Ridge. Bo sent Sun Yang to hold the province, drew all his men to Shixing, and shied from Lin's edge.

s0115.literal: Wei separately held one city, did not go to call on Bo, shut the gates and built high ramparts, and also did not resist fighting.
s0115.idiomatic: Wei held a separate city, would not call on Bo, shut the gates, piled the ramparts, and would not fight.

s0116.literal: Bo was angry and sent troops to strike Wei, seizing all his wealth, horses, and arms.
s0116.idiomatic: Bo in rage sent troops, seized all his wealth, horses, and arms.

s0117.literal: Soon he pardoned him, restored what was his, and again made alliance with him.
s0117.idiomatic: Soon he pardoned him, restored his goods, and swore alliance again.

s0118.literal: When Jingzhou fell, Wei pledged himself to Bo.
s0118.idiomatic: When Jingzhou fell, Wei pledged to Bo.

s0119.literal: When Bo crossed the mountains and came out to Nankang, he made Wei commander of the vanguard army, stationed at Bitter Bamboo Ford in Yuzhang; Zhou Wenyü broke him, captured him, and sent him to the Founder; the Founder released him and received him very generously.
s0119.idiomatic: Bo crossed to Nankang and made Wei vanguard at Bitter Bamboo Ford in Yuzhang. Zhou Wenyü broke him, sent him to the Founder, who freed him and treated him generously.

s0120.literal: After Xiao Bo died, south of the mountains was disturbed; Wei had a name in the southern lands and moreover was old friends with the Founder; he was then made Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant for Direct Communication, Commander-in-Chief of Hengzhou, Pacifier of the South General, Inspector of Hengzhou, Marquis of Shixing county.
s0120.idiomatic: After Bo died the south was in turmoil. Wei was known there and was the Founder's old friend—so he received the staff, direct-communication attendant, command of Hengzhou, pacifier-of-the-south general, inspectorship, and marquisate of Shixing.

s0121.literal: Before he reached south of the mountains, Wei's son He had already pacified Shixing.
s0121.idiomatic: Before he crossed the ridge, his son He had already taken Shixing.

s0122.literal: When Wei reached south of the mountains, all were awed and submitted; he still advanced to Guangzhou and wholly possessed the Yue lands.
s0122.idiomatic: South of the ridge all submitted in awe. He pressed on to Guangzhou and held all Yue.

s0123.literal: He was changed to Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Guang, Jiao, Yue, Cheng, Ding, Ming, Xin, Gao, He, Luo, Ai, Jiande, Yihuang, Li'an, Shishuang, and the other nineteen provinces, General Who Pacifies the South, General of the Center Who Pacifies Yue, Inspector of Guangzhou; Bearer of the Staff, Regular Attendant, and Marquis all as before.
s0123.idiomatic: He was made commander of nineteen southern provinces, general who pacifies the south, center-general who pacifies Yue, inspector of Guangzhou; staff, attendant, and marquisate unchanged.

s0124.literal: Wang Lin held the middle Yangzi; Wei by sea route and the eastern ridge sent envoys without cease.
s0124.idiomatic: Wang Lin held the middle river. Wei kept envoys moving by sea and the eastern passes.

s0125.literal: In the third year of Yongding he was advanced to Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, increased command of Hengzhou military affairs, and with his former title given Grand Precedence of the Palace.
s0125.idiomatic: In Yongding year 3 he was advanced to scattered-cavalry attendant, given more command over Hengzhou, and grand precedence with his old title.

s0126.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne he was advanced to General Who Campaigns South, changed to Duke of Yangshan commandery, fief one thousand five hundred households, and again given one set of martial music.
s0126.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded he was made general who campaigns south, Duke of Yangshan, fief fifteen hundred households, with martial music again.

s0127.literal: Earlier Inspector of Jiaozhou Yuan Tanhuan had secretly sent Wei five hundred taels of gold, ordering one hundred taels returned to Administrator of Hepu Gong Ai; Editorial footnote marker 9. four hundred taels given to his son Zhiju—others did not know of it.
s0127.idiomatic: Earlier Yuan Tanhuan of Jiaozhi had secretly left Wei five hundred taels of gold—one hundred for Hepu administrator Gong Ai [9], four hundred for his son Zhiju—unknown to anyone else.

s0128.literal: Wei was soon broken by Xiao Bo; his wealth was all gone; only the deposited gold remained.
s0128.idiomatic: Bo soon broke him and stripped him bare—only the entrusted gold remained.

s0129.literal: Tanhuan also soon died; at this Wei was able faithfully to return it; men of the time all sighed in admiration.
s0129.idiomatic: Tanhuan died too. Wei returned every ounce faithfully, and men marveled.

s0130.literal: Such was his weight on promises.
s0130.idiomatic: That was how he kept his word.

s0131.literal: At that time Wei's younger brother Sheng was Inspector of Jiaozhou, his next younger brother Sui Inspector of Hengzhou; the whole house was illustrious, their name shaking the southern lands.
s0131.idiomatic: His brother Sheng held Jiaozhi, Sui held Hengzhou—the whole clan shone, their fame ringing through the south.

s0132.literal: They also repeatedly sent bronze drums and captives, presented rare tribute; before and after it piled up and greatly aided the army and state.
s0132.idiomatic: They sent bronze drums, captives, and rare tribute in heaps that greatly fed army and state.

s0133.literal: Wei in the fourth year of Tiancheng died, aged sixty-six.
s0133.idiomatic: Wei died in Tiancheng year 4, aged sixty-six.

s0134.literal: Posthumously he was made Attendant-in-Ordinary, Chariots-and-Cavalry General, Minister of State, Inspector of Guangzhou, posthumous title Mu.
s0134.idiomatic: Posthumously: attendant-in-ordinary, chariots-and-cavalry general, minister of state, inspector of Guangzhou, posthumous name Mu.

s0136.literal: He, styled Fengsheng, had considerable ability and strategy.
s0136.idiomatic: He, styled Fengsheng, had talent and nerve.

s0137.literal: In the Tiancheng era he was made Yellow Gate Gentleman and Extraordinary Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant.
s0137.idiomatic: In the Tiancheng era he was yellow-gate gentleman and extraordinary scattered-cavalry attendant.

s0138.literal: By repeated promotion he was made Pacifier of the Distance General and Inspector of Hengzhou.
s0138.idiomatic: He rose to pacifier-of-the-distance general and inspector of Hengzhou.

s0139.literal: He inherited the dukedom of Yangshan commandery, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Jiao, Guang, and the other nineteen provinces, Inspector of Guangzhou.
s0139.idiomatic: He inherited Yangshan, commanded nineteen provinces including Jiao and Guang, and inspected Guangzhou.

s0140.literal: More than ten years in the province; his might and kindness were known among the Hundred Yue; he was advanced to Light Chariots General.
s0140.idiomatic: Ten years in the province his power and kindness were known among the Hundred Yue; he was advanced to light-chariots general.

s0141.literal: In the Guangda era, garrisons of the upper Yangzi mostly harbored second thoughts; Emperor Xuan, because He had long served in the south, quite suspected him.
s0141.idiomatic: In the Guangda era upper-Yangzi garrisons wavered. Emperor Xuan, knowing He had ruled the south long, mistrusted him.

s0142.literal: In the first year of Taijian an edict summoned He to be Left Rapid General.
s0142.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 an edict recalled him as left-rapid general.

s0143.literal: He was afraid and did not wish to obey the summons; many of his subordinates urged him to rebel; he then raised troops and attacked Inspector of Hengzhou Qian Daoji.
s0143.idiomatic: He feared the summons. His men urged revolt. He attacked Qian Daoji, inspector of Hengzhou.

s0144.literal: Daoji reported the emergency; they then sent Yitong Zhang Zhaoda to campaign against He; after repeated battles the troops were defeated; he was seized and sent to the capital, executed by beheading, aged thirty-three.
s0144.idiomatic: Daoji raised the alarm. Zhang Zhaoda was sent against him. After repeated defeats He was taken to the capital and beheaded at thirty-three.

s0145.literal: His household was registered and confiscated.

s0146.literal: His son Xun because of young age was spared.
s0146.idiomatic: His son Xun was spared for youth.

s0147.literal: Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao; Editorial footnote marker 10. was a native of Qin commandery.
s0147.idiomatic: Wu Mingche, styled Tongzhao [10], came from Qin commandery.

s0148.literal: His grandfather Jing'an was Administrator of Nanqiao in Qi.
s0148.idiomatic: His grandfather Jing'an had been administrator of Nanqiao under Qi.

s0149.literal: His father Shu was Liang Right Guard General.
s0149.idiomatic: His father Shu was Liang's right-guard general.

s0150.literal: Mingche was orphaned young, nature utmost filial; at fourteen, moved that the tombs were not yet prepared and the family was poor without means to supply it, he then labored hard at planting.
s0150.idiomatic: Orphaned young, he was filial beyond measure. At fourteen, seeing the graves unprepared and the house too poor to furnish them, he farmed with all his strength.

s0151.literal: At that time the realm was in great drought; the seedlings were scorched dry; Mingche grieved and was angry; every time he went to the fields he wept and cried out to heaven in appeal.
s0151.idiomatic: Drought scorched the fields. He wept in the furrows and cried to heaven.

s0152.literal: After several days someone returning from the fields said the seedlings had sprouted anew; Mingche doubted it, thinking himself deceived; when he went to the field place, it was exactly as the man had said.
s0152.idiomatic: After days a neighbor said the grain had greened again. Mingche did not believe it—until he walked the field and found it true.

s0153.literal: In autumn the harvest was great, enough to complete the burial.
s0153.idiomatic: That autumn the harvest filled the burial need.

s0154.literal: At that time a certain Master Yi was skilled at reading tombs; he told Mingche's elder brother: "On the day you bury, there will surely come one riding a white horse chasing a deer to pass the grave site—this is the omen of the youngest filial son attaining great honor."
s0154.idiomatic: A diviner named Yi told his brother: "On burial day a man on a white horse chasing a deer will pass the mound—that is the sign of the youngest son's greatness."

s0155.literal: When the time came there was indeed this response; Mingche was Shu's youngest son.
s0155.idiomatic: It happened as foretold. Mingche was Shu's youngest son.

s0156.literal: He began office as Eastern Palace Direct Attendant of Liang.
s0156.idiomatic: He began as direct attendant in Liang's eastern palace.

s0157.literal: When Hou Jing raided the capital the realm was in great disorder; Mingche had more than three thousand bushels of grain and millet while the whole village was starving; he then told his elder brothers: "In this age of grass-bandits men do not plan far—how can we keep this and not share with our neighbors?"
s0157.idiomatic: When Hou Jing struck the capital the land was chaos. Mingche had three thousand bushels while the village starved. He told his brothers: "Bandits roam; men live day to day—how can we hoard and not share with the lane?"

s0158.literal: He then divided by mouths, sharing alike in plenty or want; grass-bandits heard and avoided them; those who lived by it were very many.
s0158.idiomatic: He divided by mouths, rich and poor alike. Bandits heard and passed them by; many lived because of it.

s0159.literal: When the Founder garrisoned Jingkou he bound himself deeply with Mingche; Mingche then came to the Founder; the Founder for him descended a step, took his hand and sat at once, and discussed affairs of the age.
s0159.idiomatic: When the Founder held Jingkou they bound themselves close. Mingche came to him; the Founder stepped down, took his hand, sat him at once, and talked the affairs of the age.

s0160.literal: Mingche also lightly touched books, classics, and histories; he went to Zhou Hongzheng of Runan to study astronomy, void-and-solid, and escape-armor, and slightly penetrated their subtlety; he quite took himself for a hero; the Founder deeply marveled at him.
s0160.idiomatic: He skimmed the classics, studied astronomy and war-magic under Zhou Hongzheng of Runan, and thought himself born for command. The Founder marveled.

s0161.literal: In the third year of Chengsheng he was made Martial Herald General and Inspector of Anzhou.
s0161.idiomatic: In Chengsheng year 3 he was martial-herald general and inspector of Anzhou.

s0162.literal: At the beginning of Shaotai he followed Zhou Wenyü in campaigning against Du Kan and Zhang Biao and others.
s0162.idiomatic: At Shaotai's start he followed Zhou Wenyü against Du Kan, Zhang Biao, and the rest.

s0163.literal: When the eastern route was pacified he was made Bearer of the Staff, Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Pacifier of the East General, Inspector of South Yu, enfeoffed Marquis of Anwu county.
s0163.idiomatic: When the east was pacified he received the staff, scattered-cavalry attendant, pacifier-of-the-east general, inspectorship of South Yu, and marquisate of Anwu.

s0164.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate he was made Pacifier of the South General and still with Hou Andu and Zhou Wenyü led troops to campaign against Wang Lin.
s0164.idiomatic: When the Founder took the throne he was pacifier-of-the-south general and marched with Hou Andu and Zhou Wenyü against Wang Lin.

s0165.literal: When the loyal army was defeated and lost, Mingche cut his own way back to the capital.
s0165.idiomatic: When the loyal army was broken he cut his way back alone.

s0166.literal: When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne an edict added Right Rapid General to his former office.
s0166.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded an edict added right-rapid general to his rank.

s0167.literal: When Wang Lin was defeated he was made Commander-in-Chief of Wu and Yuan, Pacifier of the West General, Inspector of Wuzhou, the rest as before.
s0167.idiomatic: When Lin fell he commanded Wu and Yuan, was pacifier-of-the-west general and inspector of Wuzhou; the rest unchanged.

s0168.literal: Zhou sent the great general He Ruo Dun with more than ten thousand horse and foot to suddenly reach Wuling; Mingche's troops were few and could not match; he led the army to Baling and still broke a Zhou detached force at Shuanglin.
s0168.idiomatic: Zhou's He Ruo Dun suddenly reached Wuling with ten thousand horse and foot. Mingche, too few to stand, drew to Baling and still broke a Zhou detachment at Shuanglin.

s0169.literal: In the third year of Tiancheng he was made Pacifier of the West General.
s0169.idiomatic: In Tiancheng year 3 he was made pacifier-of-the-west general.

s0170.literal: When Zhou Di rebelled at Linchuan an edict made Mingche Pacifier of the South General, Inspector of Jiangzhou, concurrently Administrator of Yuzhang, overall commander of the army to campaign against Di.
s0170.idiomatic: When Zhou Di rebelled at Linchuan he was made pacifier-of-the-south general, inspector of Jiangzhou, concurrent administrator of Yuzhang, and overall commander against Di.

s0171.literal: Mingche by nature was upright and rigid; within his command there was not much harmony; Emperor Wen heard of it and sent the Prince of Ancheng Xu to comfort and instruct Mingche; Editorial footnote marker 11. ordering him with his former title to return to court.
s0171.idiomatic: He was stiff by nature and quarreled with his staff. Emperor Wen sent Prince Ancheng Xu to soothe him [11] and recall him at his old rank.

s0172.literal: Soon he was made General Who Guards the Front.
s0172.idiomatic: Soon he was made general who guards the front.

s0173.literal: In the fifth year he was transferred to General Who Guards the East and Administrator of Wuxing.
s0173.idiomatic: In year 5 he was transferred to general who guards the east and administrator of Wuxing.

s0174.literal: When he took leave for his commandery, Emperor Wen told Mingche: "Wuxing is only a commandery, but it is the weight of the imperial homeland—therefore I entrust it to you.
s0174.idiomatic: Taking leave for his post, Emperor Wen told him: "Wuxing is only a commandery, but it is the weight of the imperial homeland—that is why I give it to you."

s0176.literal: When Emperor Wen was ill he was summoned and made Central Palace Commander.
s0176.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen fell ill he was summoned as central palace commander.

s0177.literal: When the Last Emperor succeeded to the throne he was made Commander of the Palace Army; soon he was transferred to Intendant of Danyang; still an edict ordered Mingche to enter and leave the palace offices with forty suits of armor.
s0177.idiomatic: When the Last Emperor took the throne he was commander of the palace army, then intendant of Danyang, with forty armored men to enter the palace offices.

s0178.literal: When Dao Zhongju by forged order sent Emperor Xuan out of the capital, Mao Xi knew his plot; Emperor Xuan suspected and feared; he sent Xi and Mingche to plan together.
s0178.idiomatic: Dao Zhongju forged an order to send Emperor Xuan away. Mao Xi knew the plot; the emperor, afraid, sent Xi and Mingche to plan.

s0179.literal: Mingche told Xi: "The heir is young and in shadow; the myriad affairs have many gaps; outwardly we face strong enemies, inwardly there is great mourning.
s0179.idiomatic: Mingche told Xi: "The heir is a child in mourning. Affairs gap. Enemies press outside; mourning tears the house within."

s0180.literal: Your Highness in kinship is Zhou and Shao, in virtue you crown Yi and Huo; the altars are utmost weight—I wish you would stay at the center and plan deeply; be careful not to breed suspicion."
s0180.idiomatic: You are Zhou and Shao in kinship, Yi and Huo in virtue. The altars hang on you—stay, plan deep, and do not invite doubt."

s0181.literal: When Inspector of Xiangzhou Hua Jiao secretly harbored a different intent, an edict made Mingche Bearer of the Staff, Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of Xiang, Gui, and Wu, Pacifier of the South General, Inspector of Xiangzhou, given one set of martial music, and still with the General Who Campaigns South Chunyu Liang and others led troops to campaign against Jiao.
s0181.idiomatic: When Hua Jiao of Xiangzhou turned traitor, Mingche received the staff, scattered-cavalry attendant, command of Xiang, Gui, and Wu, pacifier-of-the-south general, inspectorship of Xiangzhou, martial music, and marched with Chunyu Liang and others against him.

s0182.literal: When Jiao was pacified he was made Grand Precedence of the Palace and advanced in rank to Duke.
s0182.idiomatic: When Jiao fell he was given grand precedence and advanced to duke.

s0183.literal: In the first year of Taijian he was made General Who Guards the South.
s0183.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 he was made general who guards the south.

s0184.literal: In the fourth year he was summoned to be Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Guards the Front, the rest as before.
s0184.idiomatic: In year 4 he was recalled as attendant-in-ordinary and general who guards the front; the rest unchanged.

s0185.literal: It happened that the court discussed a northern campaign; the dukes and ministers each differed; Mingche decided and asked to go.
s0185.idiomatic: Court debated a northern campaign. Ministers split. Mingche chose and asked to lead.

s0186.literal: In the fifth year an edict added Attendant-in-Ordinary and Commander-in-Chief of the Campaign, and still bestowed one set of women's music.
s0186.idiomatic: In year 5 he was given attendant-in-ordinary, overall command of the campaign, and a troupe of women's music.

s0187.literal: Mingche overall commanded more than a hundred thousand loyal troops, set out from the capital, and along the river cities and towns they continuously surrendered.
s0187.idiomatic: He commanded more than a hundred thousand loyal troops from the capital; river towns surrendered in line.

s0188.literal: The army reached Qin commandery and took its river barrier.
s0188.idiomatic: At Qin commandery he took the river barrier.

s0189.literal: Qi sent the great general Yuchi Pohu with troops as relief; Mingche routed him; the slain and captured could not be counted; Qin commandery then surrendered.
s0189.idiomatic: Qi sent Yuchi Pohu in relief. Mingche routed him, took uncounted heads and prisoners, and Qin surrendered.

s0190.literal: Emperor Xuan, because Qin commandery was Mingche's old district, ordered the full tai-lao sacrifice, had him worship at the shrine on the heights, civil and martial feather-banners very grand—the village took it as glory.
s0190.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan, knowing Qin was Mingche's home, ordered the grand tai-lao sacrifice. He worshiped on the heights with full civil and martial pomp—the village called it glory.

s0191.literal: Advancing he took Renzhou; he was made General Who Campaigns North, advanced in rank to Duke of Nanping commandery, fief increased together with the previous by two thousand five hundred households.
s0191.idiomatic: He took Renzhou, was made general who campaigns north, Duke of Nanping, fief increased with the previous by twenty-five hundred households.

s0192.literal: Next he pacified the two cities of Xiashi Bank and Shore.
s0192.idiomatic: Next he pacified Xiashi Bank and Shore.

s0193.literal: Pressing on to Shouyang, Qi sent Wang Lin with troops to resist and defend.
s0193.idiomatic: Pressing to Shouyang, Qi sent Wang Lin to hold it.

s0194.literal: When Lin arrived he with Inspector Wang Guixian held the outer wall.
s0194.idiomatic: Lin came and with inspector Wang Guixian held the outer wall.

s0195.literal: Mingche, because Lin had just entered and the hearts of the troops were not yet attached, attacked by night; at midnight they collapsed; Qi troops withdrew to hold the Xiangguo city and Gold city.
s0195.idiomatic: Lin had just come; hearts were not yet his. Mingche struck at night; at midnight the wall broke. Qi fell back to Xiangguo city and Gold city.

s0196.literal: Mingche ordered the army further to repair siege engines; Editorial footnote marker 12. and also dammed the Fei River to flood the city.
s0196.idiomatic: Mingche had siege engines repaired [12] and dammed the Fei to flood the town.

s0197.literal: Within the city they suffered from damp; many had belly sickness; hands and feet all swelled; those who died were six or seven in ten.
s0197.idiomatic: Inside, damp bred sickness; limbs swelled; six or seven in ten died.

s0198.literal: It happened that Qi sent the great general Pi Jinghe with several hundred thousand troops as relief, thirty li from Shouyang, encamped and did not advance.
s0198.idiomatic: Qi sent Pi Jinghe with hundreds of thousands thirty li off, camped, and would not advance.

s0199.literal: The generals all said: "The strong city is not yet taken; great relief is near—we do not know what plan my lord will bring forth?"
s0199.idiomatic: The generals said: "The city still stands and relief is near—what is your plan?"

s0200.literal: Mingche said: "In warfare speed is precious; yet they have made camp and do not advance, themselves blunting their edge—I know clearly they do not dare fight."
s0200.idiomatic: Mingche said: "War loves speed. They camp and hold—that blunts them. I know they will not fight."
